steps.title: Reasons for fitness testing
steps.body: Identify strengths and weaknesses - find out which components of fitness need improvement Monitor progress - compare test results over time to see if training is working Set baseline scores - establish starting points for setting targets and designing training programmes Compare against normative data - see how results compare to national averages for age and gender Provide motivation - give performers targets to aim for and a sense of achievement Assess suitability for a sport - determine if fitness levels meet the demands of a specific activity

steps.title: Normative data
steps.body: is a set of reference values (averages) that allow you to compare your test results against typical scores for your age and gender. Without normative data, a test score is just a number with no context.

steps.body: 1. For Fitness Testing questions, use subject-specific terminology precisely 2. Support every point with specific evidence or examples 3. Show balanced analysis — consider different perspectives before reaching a conclusion 4. Link your understanding of Fitness Testing to real-world contexts where possible 5. For longer answers, plan your response to address all parts of the question

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: You MUST know which test measures which component - this is a very common matching question Learn the basic protocol for each test (you don't need exact cone positions, but know the general procedure) Be ready to explain limitations - "not sport-specific" is the most important limitation Normative data gives CONTEXT to scores - always mention this when discussing test interpretation The Multi-Stage Fitness Test is the most commonly tested - know it in detail Understand the difference between validity (does it measure what it claims?) and reliability (is it consistent?)
